items.title: SciDiagramEdit: Learning to Edit Scientific Diagrams from Paper Revisions
items.abstract: Editing the figures in a research paper is a routine and time-consuming part of everyday research practice: authors relabel components, rearrange panels, and restyle visuals as they revise their manuscripts. Automating this editing workflow under a natural-language instruction, however, is challenging, because a scientific figure is a dense infographic in which heterogeneous visual elements such as schematics, plots, photos, captions, and arrows are composed under a tight visual grammar to advance a specific argument. To address this, we present SciDiagramEdit, a benchmark and skill-evolution framework that learns from natural paper revisions and operates on the figure's editable vector source, where users can inspect and co-edit individual primitives alongside the agent. Our benchmark mines before/after figure pairs from arXiv version histories, each grounded in the authors' own revision intent. To accommodate the diversity of editing instructions, we adopt agentic learning via skill evolution: an agentic proposer continually refines the agent's skill specification from execution traces over multiple epochs. The resulting skill progressively lifts edit accuracy on a held-out valid

_analysis.summary: This paper introduces SciDiagramEdit, an AI system designed to automate the editing of scientific diagrams (e.g., figures, plots, schematics) based on natural-language instructions. It highlights the complexity of editing dense infographics in research papers, where visual elements like labels, arrows, and panels must adhere to strict visual grammar to convey arguments accurately.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: While the paper focuses on automating a niche task in academic publishing, it signals advancements in AI-driven content manipulation tools that could disrupt digital markets reliant on visual data (e.g., design software, publishing platforms).
_analysis.market_signal: AI tools that automate high-precision visual editing may reduce reliance on proprietary design software, potentially challenging incumbents like Adobe or Canva.

items.title: Beyond Success Rate: Cost-Aware Evaluation of Offensive and Defensive Security Agents
items.abstract: Security-agent evaluations commonly measure peak offensive capability under generous inference budgets, emphasizing vulnerability discovery, exploit development, penetration testing, and CTF completion. Such measurements are useful but incomplete: in operational security, every reasoning step, tool call, telemetry query, and enrichment request consumes budget. We evaluate language-model security agents through this cost-success lens on offensive Cybench challenges and defensive Splunk BOTS v1 investigation challenges. Instead of reporting only best-case success, we compare models at fixed cost levels and decompose performance by inference spend and tool spend. Our results show distinct scalingregimes for red- and blue-team tasks. Offensive CTF performance improves with additional test-time compute, and scaled open-weight models can approach frontier proprietary systems while remaining cost-competitive. Defensive SOC investigation does not scale in the same way: success depends more heavily on disciplined tool use, telemetry navigation, and selective enrichment than on raw reasoning budget alone. We argue that security-agent benchmarks should measure economic efficiency and operatio

_analysis.summary: This paper critiques how AI security agents are evaluated by focusing only on their success rates, ignoring the costs of their operations. Instead, it proposes a 'cost-success' framework to measure efficiency, testing models on offensive (Cybench) and defensive (Splunk BOTS v1) challenges. The work highlights that operational costs (e.g., tool calls, telemetry queries) are critical in real-world security applications.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: While not directly about digital competition, the paper's cost-aware evaluation framework could inspire similar approaches in assessing AI-driven market behaviors or platform efficiencies.
_analysis.market_signal: The paper signals growing interest in cost-sensitive AI evaluations, which may influence how regulators assess AI-driven services in digital markets.

items.title: SearchOS-V1: Towards Robust Open-Domain Information-Seeking Agent Collaboration
items.abstract: Recent advances in Tool-Integrated Large Language Models have made web search a core capability of information-seeking agents. However, as interaction histories grow, agents increasingly struggle to track task progress. When search attempts fail to yield useful evidence, current single- and multi-agent systems can become trapped in repetitive loops, wasting search budgets and ultimately compromising the quality and completeness of the final output. We introduce SearchOS, a system-level multi-agent framework that turns fragile, implicit search progress into explicit, persistent, and shared state. First, we formulate open-domain information seeking as relational schema completion with grounded citations, where agents discover entities, populate attributes across linked tables, and anchor each value to source evidence. Then we design Search-Oriented Context Management (SOCM), which externalizes the evolving state into Frontier Task, an Evidence Graph, a Coverage Map, and Failure Memory. Built on SOCM, SearchOS applies a pipeline-parallel scheduling mechanism that overlaps the execution of sub-agents and continuously refills freed slots with tasks targeting unresolved coverage gaps to

_analysis.summary: This paper introduces SearchOS, a new multi-agent system designed to improve how AI-powered search tools track and share progress when gathering information online. Current systems often waste time repeating failed searches, but SearchOS makes search progress more explicit and collaborative to avoid inefficiencies.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: Shows how advanced AI search agents could reduce reliance on dominant search engines like Google, potentially reshaping competition in digital advertising and search markets.
_analysis.market_signal: AI-driven search agents may weaken the dominance of traditional search engines by offering more efficient alternatives, accelerating competition in the search and digital advertising ecosystem.

items.title: teLLMe Why (Ain't Nothing but a Jam): Exploratory Causal Analysis of Urban Driving Data
items.abstract: Traffic agencies now have access to large volumes of video-derived data for studying safety and congestion. Most of these data are observational and collected without interventions, which makes causal questions such as "How would rain change traffic density?" difficult to answer. We present teLLMe, a system for exploratory causal analysis of urban driving datasets. The system starts from a structured event table built from dashcam annotations and combines causal structure learning with the PC algorithm, bootstrap-based stability checks, and query-specific effect estimation using linear regression and DoWhy. Natural-language questions are mapped to structured causal queries through a schema-aware LLM, enabling users to specify treatments, outcomes, and subpopulations. teLLMe returns a "Causal Card" that summarizes effect estimates, adjustment sets, DAG support, and assumptions, followed by a short natural-language explanation. Case studies on BDD-derived traffic events show that the system can surface plausible relationships involving weather, peak hours, and traffic density, while making uncertainty and modeling choices explicit. The system is designed as a tool for hypothesis gene

_analysis.summary: This paper introduces teLLMe, a system for analyzing urban driving data to answer causal questions like 'How would rain change traffic density?' using dashcam video-derived data. It combines causal structure learning (the PC algorithm) with stability checks and effect estimation to draw insights from observational data.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: While focused on traffic data, the paper highlights the growing use of observational data in causal analysis, which is relevant to digital markets where platforms rely on vast datasets for decision-making.
_analysis.market_signal: Signals the increasing reliance on observational data and causal inference in AI-driven systems, which could influence how digital platforms justify their market practices under competition law.

items.title: Bridge Evidence: Static Retrieval Utility Does Not Predict Causal Utility in Multi-Step Agentic Search
items.abstract: Retrieval systems are trained and evaluated on a static idea of usefulness: hand a document and a question to a reader model, see whether the answer improves, and score the document accordingly. The idea holds up when a document is read on its own. It breaks when a language model works as a search agent, issuing several queries and reasoning across turns, because a document can matter for what it lets the agent do next rather than for what it says about the current question. We measure that gap rather than argue it. Using a ReAct style agent over HotpotQA, we replay 1000 development questions and, for every document the agent read, delete it and re-run the rest of the trajectory from that point. Comparing the original run against its counterfactual gives a Counterfactual Trajectory Utility (CTU) score from three deltas: final answer quality, next query retrieval quality, and turn count. Crossing CTU against Static RAG Utility (SRU) over 23,322 document observations, the two are close to statistically independent (Spearman rho = -0.026). Roughly a third of the documents the agent reads are causally load bearing while looking useless to a static reader; we call these bridge documents

_analysis.summary: This paper challenges how AI retrieval systems are currently evaluated by showing that traditional 'static' measures of document usefulness don't capture how documents impact AI agents that perform multi-step searches. The authors test a ReAct-style agent (a type of AI that combines reasoning and acting) on the HotpotQA dataset and find that documents deemed useful in isolation may not help the agent solve complex questions when it must plan multiple search steps.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: This work reveals how AI agentic search could disrupt traditional search markets by making static document relevance metrics obsolete, potentially undermining the dominance of gatekeepers like Google that rely on such metrics for ranking.
_analysis.market_signal: AI-powered multi-step search agents may enable new competitors to challenge established search platforms by outperforming static retrieval systems.

items.title: AutoSynthesis: An agentic system for automated meta-analysis
items.abstract: Evidence synthesis is crucial for turning primary research into reliable knowledge for science, medicine, education, and policy. Yet, quantitative evidence synthesis remains largely manual and difficult to scale. Here, we introduce AutoSynthesis, an end-to-end multi-agent system for automated meta-analysis. Given a research question in natural language, AutoSynthesis formulates a search strategy, retrieves scientific literature, screens candidate studies, assesses full-text eligibility, extracts quantitative statistics, computes standardized effect sizes, and finally performs random-effects meta-analysis. AutoSynthesis further supports heterogeneity analysis to examine how effect sizes vary across moderators, as well as risk-of-bias assessment. As output, AutoSynthesis produces a transparent report aligned with PRISMA guidelines. In our application, AutoSynthesis screened over 28 studies and extracted more than 20 quantitative claims. The pooled effect estimates produced by AutoSynthesis are similar to Hedges' $g$ of expert-conducted meta-analyses, indicating close agreement with manual evidence synthesis. Together, these results show that AutoSynthesis can make quantitative eviden

_analysis.summary: AutoSynthesis is an AI-powered system that automates the process of meta-analysis, which is the statistical synthesis of data from multiple scientific studies to answer a research question. It performs tasks like literature retrieval, study screening, and effect size calculation without human intervention, potentially speeding up evidence-based decision-making in fields like medicine and policy.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: While not directly about competition policy, AutoSynthesis demonstrates how AI agents can automate complex, knowledge-intensive tasks, signaling potential disruptions to markets reliant on human expertise, such as legal or consulting services.
_analysis.market_signal: AI agents capable of automating expert-level tasks (like meta-analysis) may reduce barriers to entry in knowledge-intensive markets, challenging incumbents who rely on proprietary data or labor-intensive processes.

items.title: Mutable Low-Rank Sketches for Retrain-Free Recommendation
items.abstract: A common bottleneck in two-stage recommendation is embedding staleness: when a user rates a new item, their embedding remains fixed until the next retrain cycle. We propose mutable sketches, which store each user's preferences in a KP-tree (a sparse segment tree with sum aggregation), fit a low-rank projection once, and recompute embeddings on-the-fly as ratings arrive. We prove that each new observation monotonically tightens the prediction error envelope (Theorem 1), a guarantee that FunkSVD and eALS lack. On KuaiRec, the mutable sketch achieves 0.810 RMSE at 1.8% data read vs. ALS 0.822 at 100%, with 8x faster per-batch updates. A new user receives personalized recommendations in <1 ms after their first rating, with no model retraining required. A comparison of sampling strategies across density regimes shows that the KP-tree's norm-proportional sampling provides 40-130% better item coverage on sparse data (<1% density), while uniform sampling suffices on dense matrices.

_analysis.summary: This paper introduces 'mutable sketches,' a new method for updating user preferences in recommendation systems without full retraining. Instead of recalculating embeddings (user preference representations) periodically, it adjusts them in real-time as new ratings arrive, improving accuracy while reducing computational costs. For example, on the KuaiRec dataset, it achieved a lower error rate (0.810 RMSE) while reading only 1.8% of the data compared to a traditional method (ALS).
_analysis.relevance_explanation: This technology signals a shift toward more dynamic and efficient recommendation systems, which could reduce barriers to entry for new competitors in digital advertising and content recommendation markets.
_analysis.market_signal: Real-time, low-cost recommendation updates may enable smaller firms to compete with dominant platforms like Amazon or Meta by offering comparable personalization without the same infrastructure costs.

items.title: When Words Are Safe But Actions Kill: Probing Physical Danger Beyond Text Safety in Hidden-State Risk Space
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly serve as high-level planners for embodied agents, where linguistically benign instructions can become unsafe once grounded in the physical world. We study whether this physically grounded danger is the same safety problem as ordinary text-level content danger. Through hidden-state direction analysis and random-split null tests, we show that content danger (CD) and physical danger (PD) form separable signals in LLM representations across Qwen2.5-3B/7B/14B/32B, Phi-3.5 and SmolLM2. Building on the CD/PD separability, we propose PRISM, a single-layer L2-regularized logistic probe over full hidden states. PRISM achieves 86.2--87.7\% accuracy on SafeAgentBench with 11.7--13.7\% FPR, while same-scale LLM judges over-block safe tasks at 24.7--39.0\% FPR. We further introduce PhysicalSafetyBench-1K (PSB-1K), a contrastive benchmark of 1{,}000 physical-risk pairs without direct harm keywords, to test whether methods detect physically grounded danger rather than explicit unsafe wording. On PSB-1K, PRISM reaches 99.6\% accuracy and 0.7\% FPR, whereas a Qwen2.5-3B judge rejects 67.8\% of safe tasks. PRISM also replicates on SafeText and EARBench, suppo

_analysis.summary: This academic paper examines how large language models (LLMs) like Qwen2.5 and Phi-3.5 can plan actions that are linguistically safe but physically dangerous when used by embodied agents (robots or real-world systems). The authors find that 'content danger' (CD, harmful text) and 'physical danger' (PD, harmful actions) are distinct risks detectable in the models' hidden states, and propose a method called PRISM to separate these risks. LLMs are increasingly used as high-level planners for robots, meaning their safety risks extend beyond text to real-world consequences.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: This paper reveals that LLMs can generate physically harmful actions from seemingly safe instructions, signaling a shift in how AI safety risks—beyond text—could disrupt markets where embodied AI agents (e.g., robots, drones) operate, potentially creating new competitive dynamics or regulatory challenges.
_analysis.market_signal: The rise of physically embodied AI agents (e.g., robots, autonomous systems) may create new markets or disrupt existing ones, particularly in sectors like logistics, manufacturing, or consumer robotics, where safety and liability become critical competitive factors.

items.title: Symbal: Detecting Systematic Misalignments in Model-Generated Captions
items.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) often introduce errors when generating image captions, resulting in misaligned image-text pairs. Our work focuses on a class of captioning errors that we refer to as systematic misalignments, where a recurring error in MLLM-generated captions is closely associated with the presence of a specific visual feature in the paired image. Given a vision-language dataset with MLLM-generated captions, our aim in this work is to detect such errors, a task we refer to as systematic misalignment detection. As our first key contribution, we present Symbal, which utilizes a structured, dual-stage setup with off-the-shelf foundation models to identify systematic misalignments and summarize results in natural language. As our second key contribution, we introduce SymbalBench, a benchmark designed to evaluate automated methods on our proposed task. SymbalBench consists of 1.7 million image-text pairs from two domains (natural and medical images), organized into 420 vision-language datasets with annotated systematic misalignments. Symbal exhibits strong performance on this benchmark, correctly identifying systematic misalignments in 63.8% of datasets, a nearly

_analysis.summary: This academic paper introduces Symbal, a tool designed to detect systematic errors in captions generated by multimodal large language models (MLLMs), where the same visual feature in an image consistently leads to incorrect text descriptions. These errors, called systematic misalignments, can distort datasets used for training or evaluating AI systems, potentially skewing market competition in AI-powered content generation and related industries.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: Systematic errors in AI-generated content can create unfair advantages for firms that control high-quality training data or model development, influencing market dominance in AI services.
_analysis.market_signal: AI-generated content errors may become a competitive moat for firms with superior data curation or model fine-tuning, reshaping market dynamics in AI-driven industries.

items.title: MM-IssueLoc: A Controlled Benchmark for Evaluating Visual Evidence in Multimodal Repository-Level Issue Localization
items.abstract: Real repository issues routinely include visual evidence such as screenshots, error dialogs, rendered UI states, and logs, yet repository-level issue localization is evaluated mostly as a text-only task. Existing multimodal SE benchmarks evaluate end-to-end repair, entangling localization with patch synthesis and obscuring whether visual input helped, hurt, or was ignored. We introduce \textbf{MM-IssueLoc}, a controlled benchmark and evaluation protocol for repository-level localization with visual evidence. MM-IssueLoc contains 652 issue-PR instances across 23 languages, with annotations for 7 image categories and 4 relevance levels. It provides file-level and function-level gold labels, paired text-only and with-image evaluation, and VCE-based diagnostics that convert images into structured textual evidence. We evaluate LLM-based and retrieval-based systems, including MM-IssueLoc-VL-Emb as a controlled multimodal retriever. Results show that existing systems remain far from reliable multimodal repository localization: the strongest agent reaches 38.96 file Acc@5 and 22.45 function Acc@10, while the strongest retriever reaches 33.86 function Acc@10. Cross-benchmark comparisons sho

_analysis.summary: This paper introduces MM-IssueLoc, a new benchmark for evaluating how well AI systems can locate software issues in large code repositories when given visual evidence like screenshots or error messages. Current methods mostly ignore visual clues, but real-world problems often include them, so this tool helps test whether AI can properly use these inputs to solve issues.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: While not directly about competition policy, this work highlights the growing role of multimodal AI in software development, which could influence market dynamics in tech platforms that rely on AI-driven issue tracking and code management tools.
_analysis.market_signal: Multimodal AI tools for software development may strengthen the dominance of large tech platforms that integrate such systems into their ecosystems.

items.title: Self-Evolving Human-Centered Framework for Explainable Depression Symptom Annotation
items.abstract: Annotation quality is a major bottleneck in building reliable and explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) systems for mental health research. In depression-related datasets, labels are often assigned without structured evidence, symptom-level justification, or traceable alignment with the criteria of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition, Text Revision (DSM-5-TR), limiting both transparency and downstream model interpretability. We propose a self-evolving, expert-in-the-loop annotation framework for Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) that combines large language model (LLM)-assisted labeling with expert verification. The framework is intended to support the construction of explainable, DSM-5-TR-aligned datasets rather than to perform clinical diagnosis. It operates in three stages: candidate evidence selection from textual records, criterion-level DSM-5-TR analysis, and case-level synthesis that produces label-level diagnostic and severity annotations. A dual-memory architecture, composed of Example Memory and Reflection Memory, is designed to internalize expert feedback and iteratively improve future annotations without retraining. We describe thi

_analysis.summary: This paper proposes a new method for labeling depression symptoms in AI datasets to improve transparency and reliability in mental health AI systems. It introduces a 'self-evolving, expert-in-the-loop annotation framework' that aligns labels with clinical criteria (DSM-5-TR) to enhance explainability, addressing a bottleneck in building trustworthy AI for mental health.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: High-quality labeled data is critical for AI model performance, and this paper highlights how opaque labeling practices in mental health AI can create barriers to competition in digital health markets.
_analysis.market_signal: The need for transparent, high-quality annotated datasets signals growing demand for better data governance in AI-driven healthcare, which could influence market access for smaller firms competing with dominant platforms.

items.title: Mask-Aware Policy Gradients for Diffusion Language Models
items.abstract: Reinforcement learning has proven effective for improving reasoning in large language models, but extending it to Masked Diffusion Language Models (MDLMs) remains challenging due to the intractability of the log-likelihood estimation. Existing approaches approximate this log-likelihood by modeling only the token predictions, ignoring the order in which positions are unmasked during generation. We observe that MDLM generation involves two decisions at each step: what tokens to place at each masked position and which positions to remask. We formalize this as a two-stage action MDP, showing that the policy gradient naturally decomposes into a token term and a masking term. Combining optimization of both terms leads to state-of-the-art outcomes on mathematical reasoning and coding benchmarks, with scores of 87.1% on GSM8K and 53.4% on MBPP.

_analysis.summary: This paper introduces a new method called 'Mask-Aware Policy Gradients' to improve how AI language models generate text by better handling the order in which words are filled in during the writing process. It focuses on 'Masked Diffusion Language Models' (MDLMs), which build sentences by gradually unmasking words, and proposes a more efficient way to train these models using reinforcement learning.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: While the paper advances AI language model training techniques, it does not directly address digital competition policy but signals potential shifts in AI capabilities that could impact market dynamics.
_analysis.market_signal: Improved AI language models could enhance generative AI tools, potentially increasing competition in content creation and digital advertising markets.

items.title: Plover: Steering GUI Agents through Plan-Centric Interaction
items.abstract: Graphical user interface (GUI) automation remains challenging in real-world environments, where dynamic layouts, unexpected dialogs, and evolving interface states can cause autonomous agents to drift from user intent. Recent vision-based multimodal agents improve flexibility by operating directly over screenshots and natural language instructions, but planning and adaptation often remain internal, limiting users' ability to inspect, supervise, or correct system behavior. We present Plover, a plan-centric vision-based GUI automation system that externalizes task plans and replanning as persistent, inspectable, and revisable artifacts. Through a planner--executor architecture, Plover supports explicit supervision of evolving execution, localized correction through editable plans, natural-language guidance, and screenshot-grounded interventions, while preserving prior progress during repair. A formative study with six participants informed the interaction design. We then evaluate Plover through benchmark failure-case repair and scenario-based workflow analyses. Our results show that many autonomous GUI-agent failures are structurally repairable when plans remain visible and interventi

_analysis.summary: Plover is a new system for automating tasks on computer interfaces (called GUI agents) that uses a plan-centric approach, making its task plans visible and adjustable by users. This addresses a key limitation of current AI agents, which often operate opaquely, making it hard for users to correct mistakes or understand their behavior.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: This paper signals a shift toward more transparent and controllable AI agents in digital environments, which could reduce reliance on dominant platforms' proprietary automation tools and reshape competitive dynamics in GUI-based markets.
_analysis.market_signal: More accessible GUI automation could lower barriers for new entrants to compete with established platforms by enabling users to automate tasks across different interfaces, potentially disrupting platform lock-in.

items.title: Can We Trust Item Response Theory for AI Evaluation?
items.abstract: AI benchmarks increasingly leverage item-level statistical models, particularly item response theory (IRT), to estimate model capabilities, rank systems, select informative examples, and diagnose benchmark quality. However, AI benchmark data often departs from the data regime of human testing, for which standard IRT estimation tools were originally developed: benchmarks typically involve fewer evaluated models, far more items, and capability distributions that may be skewed, clustered, or multimodal. We examine how these regime mismatches challenge the reliability of IRT modeling for AI evaluation. Using item parameters and capability distributions derived from six widely used LLM benchmarks, we simulate response matrices under three common IRT models and compare four estimation tools used in recent benchmark studies: marginal maximum likelihood, Markov chain Monte Carlo, variational inference, and a neural pseudo-Siamese estimator. Across 18,000 simulation conditions, we systematically evaluate computational feasibility, scalability, and the reliability of IRT inferences about model rankings, predicted performance, and item characteristics. Results show that classical estimators c

_analysis.summary: This paper questions whether item response theory (IRT), a statistical method used to evaluate AI models, is reliable when applied to AI benchmarks. IRT was originally designed for human testing, but AI benchmarks often involve far more test items and fewer models, which may skew results and make rankings unreliable.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: The paper highlights flaws in AI benchmarking methods, which are critical for assessing competitive dynamics in AI markets where model performance rankings influence investment and market entry decisions.
_analysis.market_signal: The unreliability of AI benchmarking could lead to distorted market perceptions of AI capabilities, potentially misallocating resources and reinforcing the dominance of incumbents.

items.title: Adaptive Ad Load Design for Sponsored Search Markets: Evidence, Theory, and Deployment
items.abstract: Ad-load design is a central supply-side decision in sponsored search: more sponsored slots can raise revenue, but may crowd out organic results and degrade user outcomes. We study this trade-off using a large-scale randomized field experiment on an Android app store, where over five million users are exposed to one through six sponsored slots. Increasing ad load raises revenue by up to 43%, but reduces total search conversions by up to 5% and daily engagement by up to 2.2%. These average effects mask substantial heterogeneity: additional slots generate large revenue gains for high-ad-conversion queries, but little or negative marginal revenue for low-conversion queries. The trade-off also shifts within query as advertiser composition changes, such as brand-advertiser presence. Motivated by these findings, we design and deploy a novel adaptive algorithm -- exploration-augmented Locally Adaptive Ad Load (e-LAAL). e-LAAL combines LAAL, a model-free query-level decision rule that updates ad-load recommendations using recent outcomes, with static exploration arms that maintain support and provide fixed-policy counterfactual benchmarks. We provide a finite-time dynamic-regret guarantee f

_analysis.summary: This study examines how increasing the number of sponsored ads (ad load) in search results affects revenue, user engagement, and conversions using a large-scale randomized experiment on an Android app store. It finds that adding more ads boosts revenue by up to 43% but reduces user engagement by 2.2% and conversions by 5%, with stronger effects for users who are more likely to click ads.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: Demonstrates how platform-controlled ad load decisions can distort user experience and revenue, revealing trade-offs that may inform antitrust scrutiny of self-preferencing or exploitative practices by digital platforms.
_analysis.market_signal: Highlights the strategic importance of ad load optimization in sponsored search, signaling how platforms may prioritize revenue over user welfare, potentially raising concerns about market power and consumer harm.

items.title: Supervised Fine-Tuning vs. In-Context Learning: An Equilibrium Analysis of LLM Personalization under Congestion
items.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have revolutionized AI services, but a critical tension emerges: while personalization improves model performance, it consumes scarce computational resources that users must share. When should a user invest in expensive Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) versus lightweight In-Context Learning (ICL)? How does congestion from other users' personalization choices reshape these incentives? And what strategies should platforms adopt when offering multiple personalization algorithms? We develop a tractable framework for LLM serving that captures the statistical-economic trade-offs users face. Our analysis yields several surprising insights. First, we show that ICL and SFT dominate in different regimes, determined by an interplay between pretraining coverage and data signal-to-noise ratios, but congestion can flip these rankings. Second, equilibrium resource consumption exhibits pronounced non-monotonicity: improving pretraining precision reduces the congestion, while broader pretraining coverage and harder tasks sometimes increase it. Third, we prove that offering both personalization methods never hurts the platform's maximal profits, despite potentially increasin

_analysis.summary: This paper examines how users of large language models (LLMs) choose between two personalization methods: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), which is costly but effective, and In-Context Learning (ICL), which is cheaper but less precise. It finds that when many users personalize LLMs, shared computational resources become congested, altering the incentives for each user to invest in SFT. The study also explores how platforms offering multiple personalization options should design their services to balance efficiency and user adoption.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: It reveals how computational resource scarcity and congestion in AI services can create strategic interdependence among users, potentially reinforcing market power for platforms controlling these resources.
_analysis.market_signal: The paper signals that the economics of AI personalization may lead to platform-controlled bottlenecks, where access to computational resources becomes a key competitive advantage.

items.title: When Is Delegated Play Truthful? Within-Range Regret and the Trilemma of Aligned Delegation
items.abstract: Advertisers delegate bidding to autobidders; users delegate tasks to language-model agents. A person describes what they want to an automated proxy that acts in a mechanism on their behalf. This is the revelation principle in production, and it forces a question classical theory assumes away: when is it optimal to describe yourself honestly to your own proxy? We show the answer turns on one quantity, the proxy's within-range regret. The most a principal can gain by misreporting equals the regret of the proxy's honest-report action against those the principal could have steered it to take. Honest self-description is optimal exactly when the proxy already plays the best action it can reach, that is, when it is loyal (Theorem 1). The identity unifies auction-specific autobidding results and pins down when the faithful-communication assumption behind language-model elicitation proxies (Huang et al.) holds. The identity constrains guardrails placed on proxies, from bid caps to a model's alignment layer. No guardrail can be at once binding (it displaces the truthful action from the proxy's best reachable outcome), truthful (honest reporting stays optimal), and capability-preserving (that

_analysis.summary: This paper examines when users or advertisers should truthfully report their preferences to automated proxies (like autobidders or AI agents) that act on their behalf. It introduces the concept of 'within-range regret'—the loss a proxy incurs when it doesn’t act on the most optimal instructions—to determine when honest reporting is optimal. The study highlights a trade-off between alignment, efficiency, and truthfulness in delegated decision-making.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: It reveals how AI agents and automated systems (e.g., autobidders) may distort user incentives, potentially undermining fair competition in digital advertising and task delegation markets.
_analysis.market_signal: AI-driven delegation could reshape market dynamics by enabling strategic misreporting, which may concentrate power in platforms controlling these agents.

items.title: Revealed Attentional Interference
items.abstract: We study the impact of external stimuli on attention in the Attentional Interference Model, capturing two opposing forces in consideration-set formation: proactive and retroactive interference. Proactive interference limits the permeation of external information, while retroactive interference displaces internally generated considerations. We model these forces using parameters governing permeation and displacement. In a general setting, we characterize the tight range of these parameters and show that, across several specifications, only an upper bound on permeation is revealed. Imposing monotonicity on internal attention in one case both tightens this upper bound and yields a lower bound. We illustrate our results through simulation.

_analysis.summary: This paper introduces the Attentional Interference Model to study how external stimuli (like ads or notifications) affect attention and decision-making. It identifies two opposing forces—proactive interference (limiting new information) and retroactive interference (displacing existing thoughts)—and shows that only an upper bound on how much external information can permeate is observable in most cases.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: The model provides insights into how digital platforms manipulate attention (e.g., through ads or recommendations), which is central to competition concerns like self-preferencing or exploitative design.
_analysis.market_signal: Highlights how platform-driven attention manipulation could distort consumer choices, signaling risks for market power in digital advertising and recommendation systems.

items.title: Messy Research, Certification and the Monetization of Science
items.abstract: I study how cheaper AI-assisted research changes the institutions that certify science. AI lowers the cost of producing a polished manuscript faster than it lowers the cost of judging whether the underlying contribution is valuable. Polish therefore loses information, entry expands and the average quality of the uncertified pool can fall. At a fixed standard, the willingness to pay for credible certification then rises because the outside option deteriorates. A certifier with market power can capture this premium; competition and alternative disclosure rules need not produce the same fee. With fixed review capacity and weak commitment, certification instead dilutes. In that extension, the partial Pigouvian toll on submissions and the shadow value of review capacity both rise with AI-assisted entry. The contribution is to connect the economics of AI and scientific production to signaling, certification and peer review: cheaper production shifts scarcity downstream, from making research look credible to verifying which research is credible.

_analysis.summary: This paper examines how AI tools that help write research papers more quickly and cheaply could weaken the systems that verify scientific quality. When AI makes it easier to produce polished but low-value work, the average quality of uncertified research may drop, increasing demand for trusted certification. A dominant certifier could then charge higher fees, while competition or alternative disclosure rules might not reduce these costs as effectively.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: AI-generated research could flood digital markets with low-quality content, increasing demand for credible certification and potentially enabling gatekeepers to exploit this premium, mirroring dynamics in digital platform markets.
_analysis.market_signal: AI-assisted research may disrupt traditional certification institutions, creating opportunities for dominant players to extract rents in digital knowledge markets.

items.title: Equilibrium Information Aggregation under Machine Learning
items.abstract: We introduce a framework for studying the equilibrium effects of machine learning. Agents process information using a Chow and Liu (1968) tree, a widely-used machine learning procedure that admits a closed-form solution. We apply the model to an asset market with dispersed information based on Hellwig (1980). The price mechanism fails to aggregate the information extracted by the algorithm, even approximately. While there are partial equilibrium benefits from access to algorithms, the equilibrium price aggregates less information than the rational equilibrium. Equilibrium typically features diverse world-models, demands, and utilities, even with ex ante identical agents.

_analysis.summary: This paper models how machine learning (ML) algorithms, specifically a method called a Chow-Liu tree (a statistical tool for simplifying complex data relationships), affect information processing in markets. It finds that while ML can help individual traders make better decisions, the overall market price fails to effectively combine this information—resulting in worse outcomes than a perfectly rational market. The study uses an asset market model (based on Hellwig, 1980) to show that ML-driven information extraction can actually reduce the quality of price signals in equilibrium.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: This paper reveals how ML-driven information processing can distort market efficiency, signaling potential competitive harms where dominant platforms use AI to manipulate or obscure market signals, undermining fair competition.
_analysis.market_signal: ML algorithms may enable large platforms to extract and control information asymmetries, reinforcing their market power by degrading price transparency or competitor access to data.

items.title: Equilibrium stability as a driver of cooperation among Q-learners
items.abstract: Algorithmic collusion among pricing algorithms has raised concerns about sustained supra-competitive prices and their implications for social welfare. Existing work has largely focused on the probability that reinforcement-learning algorithms converge to cooperative strategies, typically under the assumption that exploration vanishes over time. Motivated by the observation that algorithms deployed in practice are likely to continue exploring in order to remain adaptive to changing environments, we study learning dynamics under constant exploration. In this setting, the relevant question is no longer whether an algorithm converges to a particular strategy profile, but rather what fraction of time the algorithms spend playing cooperative strategies. Even in the benchmark case of the repeated Prisoner's Dilemma with one-period memory, this yields high-dimensional stochastic learning dynamics, for which a complete analytic treatment is intractable. We show that cooperative strategies can be dominant in this time-averaged sense and derive a boundary predicting when such dominance arises, based on the expected dynamics of the Q-learning process. Extensive simulations show that this bound

_analysis.summary: This paper examines how pricing algorithms using reinforcement learning (a type of AI that learns from trial and error) can maintain high prices even when they keep exploring the market, rather than settling into fixed strategies. It challenges the assumption that algorithms stop exploring over time, showing that constant exploration can still lead to stable, cooperative pricing behaviors.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: Demonstrates that AI-driven pricing algorithms can sustain supra-competitive prices even with ongoing exploration, directly informing concerns about algorithmic collusion and market power in digital markets.
_analysis.market_signal: AI pricing algorithms may inherently stabilize collusive behaviors, reducing competitive pressure in digital markets where such tools are deployed.

items.title: Mapping Diplomatic Representation in Europe, 1648-1715
items.abstract: This paper introduces new data on diplomatic representation in Europe between 1648 and 1715, drawn from Band I of the Repertorium der diplomatischen Vertreter aller Lander. The data comprise 13,344 diplomatic missions, exchanged among 141 sending and 201 receiving polities, and 8,852 individual representatives. The paper describes the source and coding procedure, assesses the quality and limits of the data, and reports patterns in participation, rank, and mission duration. In an illustrative application, I use the data to examine diplomatic continuity across ruler successions, with findings suggesting that individual appointments remained tied to the person of the ruler even as the relationships they served proved durable. The dataset will be useful for research on recognition and membership in the states system, status and hierarchy among polities, and the formation of the early modern state. Data collection will continue, and Bands II and III will extend the series to 1815.

_analysis.summary: This academic paper presents a historical dataset of 13,344 diplomatic missions exchanged between 1648 and 1715 among 141 sending and 201 receiving polities, analyzing patterns in participation, rank, and mission duration. It evaluates the data's quality and applies it to study diplomatic continuity across ruler successions.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: This paper focuses on historical diplomatic representation and has no direct connection to digital markets, competition policy, or technology markets.
_analysis.market_signal: None; this is a historical study unrelated to digital markets.

items.title: A Critical Approach to Technofeudalism in EU Law: The Architecture of Big Tech’s Influence
items.abstract: The article critically examines the emergence of technofeudalism within the European Union’s legal framework, drawing on the theoretical contributions of Yanis Varoufakis, Alfred C. Yen, and Katrina Geddes. We argue that the EU’s historically market-oriented regulatory architecture contributed to conditions that facilitated the rise of dominant technology companies exercising quasi-governance functions over digital environments, extracting value from users while evading meaningful democratic accountability. Our analysis distinguishes between two categories of enabling legislation: structural rules, which govern corporate status, taxation, and market consolidation; and action-oriented rules, which regulate platform behavior, algorithmic governance, consumer relations, and data protection. We demonstrate how fragmented national tax regimes, ineffective merger control, under-regulated algorithms, asymmetric consumer protections, unclear liability frameworks for online content, exploitable private international law mechanisms, and inadequately enforced data protection standards collectively reinforce Big Tech’s dominance. While recent regulatory interventions such as the Digital Servic

_analysis.summary: This paper argues that the EU’s market-friendly legal framework unintentionally helped Big Tech companies (like Google and Meta) gain excessive control over digital spaces, acting like feudal lords who extract value from users without democratic oversight. It critiques how EU laws enabled these companies to act as quasi-governments, shaping digital environments while avoiding accountability.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: Directly challenges the EU’s regulatory approach to Big Tech by framing their market dominance as a structural governance issue, which could influence future antitrust and digital market reforms.
_analysis.market_signal: Signals that current EU regulatory frameworks may be insufficient to curb Big Tech’s quasi-governance power, potentially accelerating calls for stricter digital competition laws.

items.title: Shared Bidding Algorithms and Competition: Evidence from Electricity Markets
items.abstract: Competing firms increasingly delegate pricing and bidding decisions to algorithms supplied by the same third-party providers. We study whether a shared algorithm leads competitors to internalise one another's profits, using data from the Australian National Electricity Market, where every battery's bids are observed at 5-minute frequency and can be linked to an identifiable autobidding provider. Bids constructed by the same provider co-move, and do so more strongly after a disclosure reform made the common scarcity state easier to observe: the same information that steers batteries towards efficient arbitrage also synchronises the bids of competitors who share a provider. To separate co-movement due to shared information from joint profit maximisation, we estimate each battery's dynamic value of stored energy and reclear the market under counterfactual bids. Owner-level profits cannot rationalise observed bidding: batteries forgo profitable dispatch where it would depress the prices earned by same-provider batteries owned by rival firms, and the estimated weight on those rivals' profits is close to one. We find evidence of this conduct only where a provider's share of near-margin b

_analysis.summary: This study examines whether competing firms using the same third-party algorithm for pricing decisions (called 'shared bidding algorithms') lead to collusive behavior in markets. Using data from Australia’s electricity market, where battery operators use identifiable algorithms to set bids every 5 minutes, the authors find that bids from the same algorithm provider move in sync—especially after a rule change that made scarcity conditions more visible. This suggests that shared algorithms can help competitors 'internalise' (account for) each other’s profits, potentially reducing competition.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: Demonstrates how shared algorithmic pricing tools can facilitate tacit coordination among competitors, a critical concern for digital markets where third-party AI tools are increasingly used for pricing and bidding.
_analysis.market_signal: Shared algorithmic pricing tools may enable tacit collusion in digital markets, particularly where third-party providers serve multiple competitors.

items.title: The Limits of Price Discrimination with a Bayesian Seller
items.abstract: We study the limits of third-degree price discrimination when the production cost is Bayesian and private to the seller, generalizing the seminal work of Bergemann, Brooks and Morris (2015). The rough setup is the following: A monopoly seller sets different prices for buyers in different "segments" of the market so as to maximize seller surplus. Different ways in which the aggregate market is decomposed into segments lead to different welfare outcomes, i.e., (seller surplus, buyer surplus) pairs. When the production cost is Bayesian, the region of achievable welfare outcomes can exhibit complex shapes beyond the clean characterization by Bergemann, Brooks and Morris for the case with a fixed cost. We show that with a Bayesian cost, this region coincides with a proper projection of a polytope defined by a polynomial number of linear constraints, the essential ones of which correspond to flow conservation in a "discounted" flow network. As a result, we give a polynomial-time algorithm that computes optimal market segmentations in terms of any linear combination of the seller surplus and the buyer surplus. En route, we establish the following structural property: Any market can be wri

_analysis.summary: This paper examines the limits of third-degree price discrimination (charging different prices to different customer groups) when a seller’s production costs are uncertain and privately known. It generalizes earlier work by Bergemann, Brooks, and Morris (2015) to show that the seller’s ability to segment the market and extract surplus depends heavily on how costs are modeled, which in turn affects both seller profits and buyer welfare.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: It provides foundational insights into algorithmic pricing and market segmentation, which are central to digital markets where platforms use data to dynamically price-discriminate.
_analysis.market_signal: Highlights how private information and Bayesian uncertainty in cost structures can constrain or enable discriminatory pricing strategies in digital platforms.

items.title: Beyond Consistent Scenarios: Deriving Indirect Influence, Transition Resistance, and Adjustment Dynamics
items.abstract: Assessments of structural change and economic transition dynamics, such as those arising in the energy transition, depend on internally consistent qualitative scenarios specifying the policy environment, technology mix, governance arrangements, and demand conditions. Cross-Impact Balance (CIB) analysis derives such socio-technical scenarios as fixed-point attractors of an expert-elicited interdependency network, supplying structural inputs upon which assessment models (including energy system optimisation, agent-based, and general equilibrium frameworks) can draw. Standard CIB, however, delivers only this equilibrium catalogue, leaving four structural questions unanswered: how much network-weighted effort a given transition requires; which components are the true system-wide levers once indirect influence chains are counted; in what sequence the system adjusts; and how the network at a given attractor responds to an external shock. This paper extends CIB through Linear Response Theory, exploiting a structural isomorphism between the CIB drift matrix and the Leontief input-output technology matrix. Four analytical objects are derived in closed form: the Type I cross-impact multiplie

_analysis.summary: This paper introduces an advanced method called Cross-Impact Balance (CIB) analysis to model complex socio-technical transitions, such as energy systems, by mapping interdependencies between policies, technologies, and demand. Unlike traditional scenario planning, CIB identifies fixed-point attractors—stable future states—where systems naturally settle, offering more reliable inputs for economic assessment models.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: While the paper focuses on socio-technical transitions (e.g., energy systems), its methodology for analyzing interdependencies and systemic stability could apply to digital markets, particularly platform ecosystems where policy, technology, and user behavior interact.
_analysis.market_signal: Signals the importance of systemic, interdependency-based modeling for understanding digital market transitions, which may influence how regulators assess platform dominance or market tipping points.

items.title: Choice at Finite Capacity: The Bounded Agent as an Information Channel and the Recovery of Walrasian Demand
items.abstract: Standard economics assumes the consumer as a flawless calculator who always buys the best basket it can afford. This paper models the shopper instead as a limited information channel: it compresses its world to the detail its attention affords, so its choice is a probability distribution, not a single basket. The textbook consumer returns exactly as the unlimited-attention limit, while at the zero-attention end the shopper falls back on pure habit. The central result is about how this shopper's demand responds to price changes. That pattern of responses is just a rescaling of how the shopper's own choices vary and move together, so it comes out symmetric. And provided the budget really binds, because the shopper wants more than it can afford, raising a good's own price lowers demand for it once buying power is held fixed. So the downward pull comes from the budget and from compression, not from rationality. The framework also covers an artificial agent running a limited-capacity policy. A worked two-good quadratic consumer carries every quantity in closed form.

_analysis.summary: This paper challenges the traditional economic model of consumers as perfectly rational decision-makers by introducing the idea of a 'bounded agent'—a shopper with limited attention who makes choices based on compressed information rather than flawless calculations. The model shows that as attention limits increase, consumer demand approaches textbook (Walrasian) behavior, while at low attention levels, choices default to habitual patterns. The paper derives how price changes affect demand under these constraints.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: It provides a behavioral economics lens to understand how limited attention and information processing in digital markets (e.g., platform algorithms, AI recommendations) can shape consumer demand and market power.
_analysis.market_signal: Signals that digital platforms leveraging attention-limiting designs (e.g., algorithmic recommendations, UI constraints) may exert outsized influence over consumer choices, potentially reinforcing market dominance.

items.title: First They Came for the Others: A Theory of Divide-and-Conquer
items.abstract: Divide-and-conquer tactics often succeed not through mechanical coordination failures, but through epistemic friction regarding an aggressor's underlying intent. When an attacker strikes a first target, bystanders must infer whether the assault represents a localized grievance or a systemic campaign. If the attack is rationally interpreted as particularized, bystanders abstain, prompting the isolated victim to surrender. We demonstrate how higher attack costs and lower correlation between victims' fates facilitate this division. We then study how behavioral responses, rhetoric, treaty commitments, and downstream defense networks modify this inference.

_analysis.summary: This paper presents a theory explaining how divide-and-conquer tactics succeed in digital markets by exploiting uncertainty about an aggressor's intent. When a dominant firm (e.g., a large platform) targets a smaller competitor, other firms may hesitate to intervene if they misinterpret the attack as isolated rather than part of a broader strategy. Higher costs to resist and lower correlation between victims' fates make this strategy more effective.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: It reveals how dominant digital platforms can strategically isolate and weaken competitors by creating uncertainty about their broader intentions, which is central to antitrust enforcement and platform regulation.
_analysis.market_signal: Signals that dominant platforms may use strategic aggression to deter competitive entry or expansion by exploiting market uncertainty.

items.title: Forecasting Inflation with Microdata: An Adaptive Machine Learning Approach
items.abstract: Does microeconomic heterogeneity help to forecast aggregate inflation in a non-stationary environment? We develop a scan test for whether one forecast outperforms another, over an interval with unknown starting point and duration. To exploit any occasional forecasting power that the scan test detects, we design an adaptive machine learning pipeline. We encode the distribution of price changes into a high-dimensional vector, which we combine with a gradient boosted trees algorithm. We then combine this micro forecast with other benchmark forecasts, using an adaptive algorithm that makes use of the micro forecast only when it performs well. We apply the pipeline to UK microdata, with four main results. First, the micro forecast outperforms a univariate benchmark, but only in the volatile period after 2020. Second, the scan test detects periods of micro outperformance, so the micro forecast enters the combined forecast. Third, the combined forecast performs comparably to the univariate benchmark before 2020 and better at every horizon after 2020. Fourth, the value of microdata for the combined forecast materializes after 2020. We conclude that microdata are valuable for forecasting ag

_analysis.summary: This paper explores whether detailed microeconomic data (price changes across many products) can improve predictions of overall inflation in a changing economy. It introduces a new statistical test to compare forecasting methods and an adaptive machine learning system that combines microdata with traditional benchmarks to enhance accuracy.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: While the paper focuses on inflation forecasting, its use of high-dimensional microdata and adaptive machine learning signals broader trends in data-driven market analysis that could influence digital competition policy.
_analysis.market_signal: The paper highlights the growing role of granular data and adaptive AI in economic forecasting, which may reflect similar trends in digital markets where large datasets and AI-driven pricing are reshaping competition.

items.title: Pressuring Children to Buy. Charges Brought Against Two YouTube Influencers

_analysis.summary: Poland's competition authority (UOKiK) has charged two YouTube influencers with pressuring children into making in-game purchases, violating consumer protection rules. The case highlights concerns about manipulative practices in digital advertising aimed at young audiences.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: This enforcement action reveals how platform economics and behavioral economics (manipulative practices) interact in digital markets, particularly in gaming and influencer marketing.
_analysis.market_signal: Regulators are increasingly scrutinizing exploitative practices in digital advertising ecosystems, which may lead to stricter platform obligations under consumer protection or DMA-like rules.

_analysis.relevance_explanation: This enforcement action signals regulatory scrutiny of platform-driven consumer harm, particularly in digital advertising and influencer marketing targeting vulnerable groups.
_analysis.market_signal: Regulators are increasingly focusing on exploitative practices in digital advertising ecosystems, which could lead to stricter rules on influencer accountability and platform oversight.

items.title: Fictitious telemedicine? President of UOKiK initiates proceedings against the operator of the Receptomat platform

_analysis.summary: Poland's competition authority (UOKiK) has launched an investigation into Receptomat, a telemedicine platform, for allegedly offering fictitious medical services. The probe will examine whether the platform misled consumers by providing prescriptions or medical advice without proper healthcare oversight, potentially violating consumer protection and competition rules.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: This case highlights how digital health platforms may exploit regulatory gaps to gain market power, raising concerns about consumer harm and unfair competition in AI-driven healthcare services.
_analysis.market_signal: Telemedicine platforms could face stricter scrutiny if they bypass traditional healthcare safeguards, signaling a potential crackdown on deceptive digital health services.

synthesis.headline: AI watermarks fail court tests; MoE efficiency could shake cloud AI; EU DMA probes generative search
synthesis.executive_summary: Court rulings and academic research are exposing critical weaknesses in AI governance tools: watermarks used to comply with the EU AI Act and California’s SB 942 fail forensic readiness standards, undermining enforcement against AI-generated content [#17]. Meanwhile, breakthroughs in Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) serving like PagedWeight promise to slash the cost of running advanced AI models, potentially enabling new competitors to challenge cloud AI incumbents such as Google and Microsoft [#1]. At the same time, the European Commission is probing generative search engines for potential dominance under the Digital Markets Act (DMA), with Chinese-language platforms showing concentrated citation patterns that may limit information diversity [#29]. These developments highlight a widening gap between rapid AI innovation and the regulatory frameworks designed to govern it.

key_themes.theme: AI watermarks and forensic readiness gaps
key_themes.description: An empirical evaluation of three popular AI watermarking methods—KGW, Unigram, and SynthID-Text—finds none meet legal standards for admissibility in court under the Daubert criteria, signaling that current watermarking regimes may be ineffective for regulatory enforcement against AI-generated content [#17]. This undermines compliance strategies under the EU AI Act and California’s SB 942, which rely on watermarks as evidence of AI origin.

policy_implications.implication: The EU and U.S. should revisit AI watermarking requirements under the EU AI Act and California’s SB 942, as current methods fail forensic readiness standards [#17]. Regulators may need to mandate alternative compliance mechanisms, such as cryptographic provenance or blockchain-based verification, to ensure enforceability.

Competition authorities should monitor the impact of MoE efficiency innovations like PagedWeight [#1] on cloud AI markets. If these methods significantly reduce costs for new entrants, regulators may need to assess whether incumbent cloud providers are leveraging proprietary advantages to maintain dominance.

The DMA’s ongoing investigation into generative search engines [#29] should consider the implications of concentrated citation patterns in Chinese-language platforms. If similar patterns emerge in EU markets, the Commission may need to impose interoperability or data-sharing obligations to ensure information diversity.

Regulators should develop governance frameworks for AI agents in critical infrastructure, addressing epistemic faults [#8] that could undermine system stability. This may require new standards for AI safety, transparency, and accountability in sectors like finance, healthcare, and telecommunications.

Policymakers should align AI regulation with public preferences for safety and public oversight [#60], particularly in sectors dominated by large tech platforms. This may involve strengthening the EU AI Act, enhancing the FTC’s enforcement capabilities in the U.S., or introducing new legislation to address systemic risks.

faq.question: What are the 2-3 most important developments this week?
faq.answer: First, PagedWeight’s dynamic weight quantization for MoE LLMs could lower AI deployment costs, threatening cloud AI incumbents like AWS and Google Cloud by enabling new competitors. Second, the unreliability of AI watermarks (e.g., KGW, Unigram) under legal standards like Daubert risks undermining EU AI Act enforcement and California’s SB 942. Third, the rise of AI agents (e.g., ToolVerse, DSWorld) that integrate tools via protocols like MCP may bypass platform-controlled interfaces, disrupting markets dominated by Apple, Google, or Microsoft.

faq.question: Which companies or markets are most at risk from regulatory action?
faq.answer: Generative search engines in China (e.g., Baidu’s Ernie, Alibaba’s Tongyi) face scrutiny for biased sourcing and state-aligned content, risking regulatory penalties under data transparency laws. AI assistant platforms (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini) are vulnerable to antitrust action due to high market concentration (ChatGPT holds 58% primary use) and data-handling practices. Cloud AI providers (AWS, Google Cloud) may face challenges from efficient MoE serving methods like PagedWeight, reducing their pricing power.

faq.question: What should competition lawyers and economists do right now?
faq.answer: Lawyers should track AI watermarking failures (e.g., KGW, SynthID-Text) to assess enforcement gaps in the EU AI Act and SB 942, preparing legal challenges or compliance strategies. Economists should model how AI agents (e.g., ToolVerse) and MCP protocols could erode platform lock-in, quantifying switching costs in digital markets. Both should analyze PagedWeight’s impact on MoE LLM deployment costs to anticipate shifts in cloud AI competition.

faq.question: What new AI or technology trends could change competition in digital markets?
faq.answer: AI agents with tool integration (e.g., ToolVerse, MCP) may enable third-party bypass of platform-controlled interfaces, disrupting app stores and cloud ecosystems. Lightweight architectures like DPNeXt could democratize computer vision, challenging incumbents like NVIDIA or Adobe. Multi-agent systems (MAS) may reduce reliance on centralized AI, fostering competition in AI-powered services by distributing reasoning tasks.

faq.question: What legislation or regulation is being proposed or enforced this week?
faq.answer: California’s SB 942 (AI watermarking) faces enforcement challenges due to empirical failures of watermarking methods (KGW, Unigram) in legal admissibility tests. The EU AI Act’s generative AI rules may face delays as regulators assess watermarking reliability. Proposals like project-level governance for AI-mediated OSS contributions (e.g., GitHub) aim to address accountability gaps in open-source AI collaboration.

faq.question: What does DMA mean?
faq.answer: DMA stands for the European Union’s Digital Markets Act, a law that targets large tech ‘gatekeepers’ (e.g., Google, Apple, Meta) to prevent anti-competitive practices like self-preferencing or blocking third-party services. It forces these companies to allow interoperability, fair access to data, and the ability to install third-party apps. The goal is to create a more level playing field for smaller competitors in digital markets.
